| [LIT-786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-786.md) | On Linguistic Aspects of Translation | Jakobson (1959), in Brower (ed.), On Translation, Harvard University Press, pp. 232–239. The meaning of a sign is its translation into further signs; translation is intralingual, interlingual or intersemiotic. Code-units rarely have full equivalents across languages, but messages can be adequately rendered: "equivalence in difference" is the cardinal problem. All cognitive content is conveyable in any language; languages differ in what they must convey, so obligatory categories force choices that add or drop information. Poetry, where grammar and sound carry meaning, allows only creative transposition. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-614](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-614.md)): in full, from a scan of the 1959 printing posted as a course reading by the University of Toronto's Centre for Comparative Literature. Worth reading as the source of the three kinds of translation (intralingual, interlingual, intersemiotic) and of the argument that interlingual translation substitutes whole messages for messages, since code-units rarely have full equivalents. Its sharpest claim is that languages differ in what they must convey, not in what they may convey: obligatory grammatical categories force a translator to add or drop information, so a chain of translations back and forth can strip a message of its content. Limits: an essay argued from examples, with one psychological test cited second-hand; poetry is set aside as untranslatable, open only to "creative transposition". |

Read it knowing that its models are uniform, random and lossless, that the bounds are information-theoretic, and that the prior substitutes for parallel data in learning a decoder, not for information in a message. | [LIT-1303](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1303.md) | Worth a Thousand Words: The Images of Copyright | Tushnet (2012). Copyright takes the written word as its model. Courts treat images either as transparent, so that their meaning is obvious and they merely copy reality, or as opaque, so that they cannot be analysed in words. The oscillation produces incoherent doctrine on copyrightability, substantial similarity, joint authorship of comics and fair use. Verbal overshadowing means that describing an image changes how it is seen, so the substantial-similarity test should be abandoned for a reproduction right against exact or near-exact copies. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1016](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1016.md)) in full; worth reading as the standard statement that copyright law takes the written word as its model and so oscillates between treating images as transparent (their meaning obvious, a copy of reality) and as opaque (beyond analysis in words), of verbal overshadowing as a reason the substantial-similarity test cannot work, and of the proposal to replace that test with a reproduction right against exact or near-exact copies, leaving the rest to the derivative-works right. Read it knowing that it is US law as of 2011, that the cognitive findings are cited from the psychology literature rather than tested on legal factfinders, that the author flags the verbal-overshadowing effect as possibly smaller than first reported, and that the reform is stated without its implementation (n. 258). |

| [LIT-1845](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1845.md) | Translation and Relevance | Gutt (1989), PhD thesis, University College London. Translation needs no theory of its own: it is interlingual interpretive use under Sperber and Wilson's relevance theory. Two utterances interpretively resemble each other to the degree that the explicatures and implicatures each conveys in its own cognitive environment overlap, and a translation is faithful when it resembles the original closely enough in the respects that make it adequately relevant to its audience, at no gratuitous processing cost. Direct translation, which preserves the original's communicative clues, is the limiting case: complete interpretive resemblance in the cognitive environment the original envisaged. The precursor of the 1991 book ([LIT-784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-784.md)). | Active — skimmed 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1435](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1435.md)) from the UCL Discovery eprint (discovery.ucl.ac.uk/1317504/1/241978.pdf, 309 pp., OCR text layer): the abstract, preface and contents, the critique of functional equivalence (pp. 22–27), the relevance-theoretic chapter's account of interpretive resemblance (pp. 50–76), the critique of dynamic equivalence (pp. 118–130), all of chapter 5 on faithfulness as optimal resemblance (pp. 160–193), all of chapter 6 on communicative clues (pp. 194–248) and the opening of chapter 7 with its definition of direct translation (pp. 249–257). The rest is unread. Worth reading as the thesis that became Translation and Relevance ([LIT-784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-784.md)), and as the only reading of Gutt's account the record holds. On it, two utterances interpretively resemble each other to the degree that the assumptions each communicates in its own cognitive environment overlap, so resemblance is judged by what is communicated, not by wording or propositional form. A translation is faithful when it resembles the original closely enough in the respects that make it relevant to its audience. Direct translation is the limiting case, complete interpretive resemblance in the context the original envisaged. Read it as the 1989 thesis, not the book: what the book changed is unread. |
| [LIT-1863](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1863.md) | Translating as a purposeful activity: a prospective approach | Nord (2005), TradTerm 11:15–28. A short statement of functionalist translation. Since a text is an offer of information that different receivers take differently, the translator works prospectively, toward the purpose the translation is to serve for a target audience under the brief. Communicative purposes are phatic, referential, expressive and appellative. Where target-culture conditions differ, each function is either adapted so it works (instrumental translation) or turned into a meta-function that explains how it worked (documentary translation), and the brief, not a general preference, decides which. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1448](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1448.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF on the TradTerm site (periodicos.usp.br/tradterm/article/download/49673/53784/61052, 14 pp.). Worth reading as Nord's own short statement of functionalist translation, the record's only reading of the functional account while her book ([LIT-829](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-829.md)) is unread. A text is an offer of information, which different receivers take differently, so the translator works prospectively, toward the purpose the translation is to serve for a particular target audience as the brief specifies. Nord sorts communicative purposes into phatic, referential, expressive and appellative functions. Where target-culture conditions differ, the translator either adapts the text so that the function works (instrumental translation) or turns it into a meta-function that tells the audience how the original worked (documentary translation). Neither is better in general: the brief decides. Equivalence is often "not required or not even desired". |
| [LIT-1864](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1864.md) | Principles of Correspondence | Nida (1964), "Principles of Correspondence", abridged in Venuti (ed.), The Translation Studies Reader, 2nd ed. (2004), pp. 126–140. There is no exact translation, only closest equivalents, and there are two orientations. Formal equivalence reproduces the message's form and content, as in a gloss translation with notes. Dynamic equivalence, "the closest natural equivalent to the source-language message", aims at a receptor–message relationship "substantially the same" as the original receptors had, and so at a similar response. It must still reflect the source's meaning and intent, and meaning comes before style. Its example is Phillips's handshake for the "holy kiss" of Romans 16:16. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1451.md)) from a course-reading PDF of the reprint (newuniversityinexileconsortium.org, "Week-6-Dynamic-equivalence-and-formal-equivalence-Nida-1964-in-Venuti-2004-1.pdf", 15 pp., Reader pp. 126–140). Worth reading as the record's only first-hand text of Nida's two orientations, while Toward a Science of Translating ([LIT-791](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-791.md)), whose chapter this abridges, is unread. Formal equivalence matches the message in form and content. Dynamic equivalence aims at "the principle of equivalent effect": "the relationship between receptor and message should be substantially the same as that which existed between the original receptors and the message". Nida's example is Phillips's "hearty handshake all around" for Romans 16:16's "holy kiss". A dynamic-equivalence translation is "the closest natural equivalent to the source-language message". It must still "clearly reflect the meaning and intent of the source", and meaning takes priority over style. Read it as an abridgement whose cuts are not marked. |
